job.system:
You are the AI assistant for the Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: The Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining (CADM) is a nonprofit advocacy organization based in Washington, DC. We believe that the industrial mining of the deep seabed, meaning the large-scale extraction of minerals from the ocean floor, poses a serious risk of irreversible destruction to deep-ocean ecosystems, and that no one currently knows how to conduct it without such damage. Our goal is a legally binding prohibition on commercial deep-sea mining, first in the United States and then through an international treaty. We work through lobbying, grassroots organizing, and public education.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which we strongly support. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
**Top priorities for Thursday:** #1, #2, #4, #10–11, and #18.

1. **§7(b) (sunset):** The Act "shall cease to have effect" 10 years after enactment, regardless of any finding. This contradicts §7(a)'s "remain in effect until" language and would let the prohibition lapse automatically. Strike it, or make it conditional, and specify which subsection controls.

2. **§7(a) (trigger):** "Serious harm" is undefined, and the trigger is that mining "can be conducted without serious harm," a low bar that a joint resolution could meet on a thin record. Define the standard and require a specific finding on the NASEM report's content.

3. **§7(a) (procedure):** The text doesn't say whether the joint resolution goes through presentment to the President, whether it has expedited procedures, or when the NASEM report is due. Without a deadline, the trigger may never occur, and without presentment, the mechanism may be challenged.

4. **§2(1)(A) (tonnage threshold):** The 10,000-ton limit applies to "a single vessel," so operators can split activity across multiple vessels, affiliates, or years, or stay just under the limit. Aggregate across all vessels and affiliated operators, and measure cumulatively per project.

5. **§2(1)(A) (depth floor):** The 200-meter floor excludes shelf-depth recovery, and "seabed" and "mineral resources" are undefined. Clarify whether shallower recovery is intended to be covered, or define the scope by reference to the deep seabed.

6. **§2(1)(A) ("recovery"):** The definition only counts tonnage recovered, so sediment plumes, bottom disturbance, and discharges that don't result in recovered material fall outside it. Add an impact-based prong or define "recovery" to include associated disturbance and discharge.

7. **§2(1)(B) ("the Secretary"):** "Secretary" is undefined, so it's unclear which department decides, and the determination has no criteria, procedure, notice, or record requirement. This invites both a vagueness challenge and discretionary exemptions. Name the official and add standards and a process, or delete the provision.

8. **§2(1)(B) ("comparable"):** "Comparable" has no benchmark, so the catch-all can't be applied predictably. Tie it to specific measurable criteria such as disturbance area, plume volume, or habitat impact.

9. **§2(2) ("U.S. person"):** The definition covers only citizens and corporations organized under state law. It excludes LLCs, partnerships, and foreign-incorporated subsidiaries of U.S. companies, and "State" is undefined (DC and territories are unclear). Add entities controlled by U.S. persons and define "State."

10. **§3(a) (territorial scope):** "In the United States" doesn't clearly reach the EEZ, the continental shelf, or the high seas. Foreign-flagged vessels operated by non-U.S. persons beyond U.S. waters appear to be outside the prohibition.

11. **§3(a) (missing ancillary prohibitions):** The bill doesn't prohibit financing, insurance, procurement, processing, importation, or sale of deep-sea minerals, or aiding and abetting. Without these, operators can use foreign vessels and sell the product in the U.S.

12. **§3(a) ("engage in"):** "Engage in" is undefined, so it's unclear whether equipment testing, deployment, and pre-mining preparation count. Define the term to cover preparatory and support activities.

13. **§3(b) ("exploration license"):** The term isn't defined or tied to any issuing authority, so it may refer to ISA contracts, NOAA permits, or something else. The exemption also covers "mining conducted under" an exploration license, which could be read to permit commercial recovery. Add an express bar on commercial recovery, a sunset date for grandfathered authority, and disclosure requirements.

14. **§3(c) (environmental assessment exemption):** There's no cap on tonnage, duration, or sale of recovered material, and "for the purpose of" is subjective. Operators could relabel commercial mining as assessment. Require advance approval, a volume cap, reporting, and a bar on sale or export.

15. **§4(a) (registration):** "Operator" is undefined, there's no deadline to register before operating, and §5 doesn't penalize registration failures because it only covers §3 violations. Add a registration penalty and a pre-operation filing deadline.

16. **§4(b) (reports):** The reports have no content requirements (tonnage, location, depth, discharges, incidents), no public-disclosure requirement, no verification or audit authority, and no fixed filing deadline. Specify required content and make reports public.

17. **§4 (registry scope):** The registry covers only "covered vessels" (§2(3)), so smaller vessels that conduct recovery under an exemption have no reporting obligation at all. Extend registration and reporting to any vessel conducting recovery activity.

18. **§5(a) vs. §8 (effective-date mismatch):** Civil penalties apply to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but §3 takes effect 180 days later under §8. That gap invites an argument that no violation is possible until day 180. Tie the penalty effective date to §8.

19. **§5 (enforcement architecture):** The bill doesn't designate an enforcing agency, authorize injunctions, provide for seizure or forfeiture of vessels, equipment, or minerals, create a citizen-suit provision, or set a limitations period. It also doesn't say how daily violations are counted (per vessel, per day, or per ton) or address corporate officer liability.

20. **§5(a) (penalty amount):** The $1,000,000-per-day penalty isn't inflation-adjusted and has no per-ton or gain-based alternative. Large operators could treat it as a cost of doing business. Consider adding a gain-based or per-ton penalty and an inflation adjustment.

21. **§5(b) ("willfully"):** "Willfully" is undefined, and the criminal provision doesn't cover §4 violations such as false or missing reports. Add a false-statements offense and define the mens rea standard.

22. **§6 ("shall seek to negotiate"):** The provision creates no obligation to conclude an agreement and no consequence if the 18-month target is missed. "Equivalent" is undefined, and there's no coordination requirement with the ISA or UNCLOS, which invites a treaty-conflict challenge. Add reporting, define "equivalent," and include a savings clause.

23. **General provisions (missing):** The bill has no severability clause, so striking one section could bring down the penalty structure with it. It also lacks a savings clause for treaty obligations, rulemaking authority, an appropriations provision, and any judicial review or preemption language. Add a severability clause and rulemaking authority at a minimum.

24. **§8 (effective date and interim gap):** The 180-day delay combined with the §3(b) grandfathering creates a window for operators to ramp up before the prohibition applies. Consider a moratorium on new exploration licenses and permits effective on enactment.

**Caveats:** I reviewed only the text you provided. I haven't checked it against the pre-amendment text, DSHMRA, UNCLOS, or ISA rules, and some items above depend on how those interact with this bill. Have Senate Commerce or CRS counsel check the cross-references and the legal conclusions before anything is filed. If you'd like, I can draft replacement language for any of these, starting with §§7(a)–(b) and 2(1)(A).
